paragraphs: For as long as the Achaeans and Trojans were fighting around the wall and had not yet got inside it or reached the ships, Patroclus stayed sitting in the tent of good Eurypylus. He kept him company with his talk and spread herbs over his wound to ease the pain. But then he saw the Trojans swarming through the breach in the wall while the Achaeans screamed in panic. He cried out and struck both his thighs with the flat of his hands. “Eurypylus,” he said in dismay, “I know you need me badly, but I cannot stay with you any longer, because the fighting has turned hard. A servant will look after you now. I must hurry to Achilles and try to get him to fight. Who knows, with the help of heaven I may persuade him. A man does well to listen to a friend’s advice.”

With that he went on his way. The Achaeans held firm against the Trojan attack. The Trojans were fewer in number, yet the Achaeans could not push them back from the ships, and the Trojans could not break the Achaean ranks and force their way in among the tents and ships. A carpenter’s line gives a true edge to a piece of ship’s timber in the hand of a skilled workman, whom Athena has taught all kinds of useful arts. In the same way the fight between the two sides stayed level, as they fought, some around one ship and some around another.

Hector went straight for Ajax, and the two of them fought fiercely around the same ship. Hector could not push Ajax back and set the ship on fire, and Ajax could not drive Hector away from the spot where heaven had brought him.

Then Ajax struck Caletor son of Clytius in the chest with his spear as Caletor was carrying fire toward the ship. Caletor fell heavily to the ground, and the torch dropped from his hand. Hector saw his cousin lying in front of the ship and shouted to the Trojans and Lycians. “Trojans, Lycians, and Dardanians good in close fight, do not give up an inch of ground. Rescue the son of Clytius, or the Achaeans will strip him of his armor now that he has fallen.”

Then he threw a spear at Ajax and missed him. But he hit Lycophron, a follower of Ajax. Lycophron came from Cythera, and he lived with Ajax because he had killed a man among the Cythereans. Hector’s spear struck him on the head below the ear, and he fell headlong from the ship’s prow to the ground, with no life left in him. Ajax shook with rage and spoke to his brother. “Teucer, my good fellow, our trusted comrade the son of Mastor has fallen. He came from Cythera to live with us, and we honored him as much as our own parents. Hector has just killed him. Quickly, fetch your deadly arrows and the bow that Phoebus Apollo gave you.”

Teucer heard him and hurried to his side with his bow and quiver in his hands. At once he sent a shower of arrows at the Trojans. He hit Cleitus son of Pisenor, a comrade of Polydamas, the noble son of Panthous. Cleitus had the reins in his hands and was tending his horses. He was in the very thickest part of the fight, doing good service to Hector and the Trojans, but now evil had come upon him, and none of those who wanted to could keep it off him, because the arrow struck him on the back of the neck. He fell from his chariot, and his horses swerved aside and shook the empty car. King Polydamas saw what had happened and was the first to reach the horses. He put them in the charge of Astynous son of Protiaon and ordered him to watch and keep the horses close at hand. Then he went back and took his place in the front ranks.

Teucer then aimed another arrow at Hector. If he had hit and killed him there and then, there would have been no more fighting at the ships. But Zeus, who watched over Hector, kept his eyes on Teucer and robbed him of his triumph. Just as Teucer was drawing the bow and about to take aim, Zeus broke the bowstring. The arrow went astray and the bow dropped from his hands. Teucer shook with anger and spoke to his brother. “Alas, see how heaven thwarts us in everything we do. It has broken my bowstring and snatched the bow from my hand, though I strung it this very morning so that it would serve me for many arrows.”

Ajax son of Telamon answered, “My good fellow, leave your bow and your arrows alone, because Zeus has made them useless to spite the Danaans. Take your spear, put your shield on your shoulder, and fight the Trojans yourself and urge the others to fight too. They may be winning for the moment, but if we fight as we ought, they will find the ships hard to take.”

Teucer then took his bow and put it away in his tent. He hung a shield four hides thick from his shoulders, and on his fine head he set a well-made helmet with a crest of horse-hair that nodded menacingly above it. He took up his formidable bronze-tipped spear, and at once he was at Ajax’s side.

Hector saw that Teucer’s bow was no use to him any more, and he shouted to the Trojans and Lycians. “Trojans, Lycians, and Dardanians good in close fight, be men, my friends, and show your courage here at the ships. I have seen the weapon of one of their chieftains made useless by the hand of Zeus. It is easy to tell when Zeus is helping people and means to help them still more, and again when he is bringing them down and will do nothing for them. Now he is on our side and is turning against the Argives. So swarm around the ships and fight. If any of you is struck by spear or sword and loses his life, let him die. A man who dies fighting for his country dies with honor. He leaves his wife and children safe behind him, and his house and allotment unplundered, if only the Achaeans can be driven back to their own land, they and their ships.”

With these words he put heart and soul into all of them. On the other side Ajax urged on his comrades. “Shame on you, Argives! Now we are utterly lost unless we can save ourselves by driving the enemy from our ships. If Hector takes them, do you think you will get home by land? Can you not hear him cheering on his whole army to set our fleet on fire? He tells them to remember that they are in a battle, not at a dance. Our only course is to fight them with all our strength. We had better take our chance, life or death, once and for all, than be hemmed in at our ships by worse men than ourselves and fight a long time with no result.”

With these words he put life and soul into all of them. Then Hector killed Schedius son of Perimedes, leader of the Phoceans, and Ajax killed Laodamas, a captain of foot soldiers and son of Antenor. Polydamas killed Otus of Cyllene, a comrade of the son of Phyleus and chief of the proud Epeans. Meges saw this and sprang at Polydamas, but Polydamas crouched down and Meges missed him, because Apollo would not allow the son of Panthous to fall in battle. The spear hit Croesmus in the middle of the chest instead, and he fell heavily to the ground, and Meges stripped him of his armor. At that moment the valiant soldier Dolops son of Lampus charged in. Lampus was a son of Laomedon and famous for his valor, and his son Dolops knew every way of war. Dolops attacked at close quarters and struck the middle of the shield of the son of Phyleus with his spear, but his good corslet, made with plates of metal, saved him. Phyleus had brought it from Ephyra and the river Selleis, where his host, King Euphetes, had given it to him to wear in battle for protection. Now it saved the life of his son. Then Meges struck the topmost crest of Dolops’s bronze helmet with his spear and tore off its plume of horse-hair. It had just been dyed scarlet, and it tumbled into the dust. Dolops was still fighting, confident of victory, when Menelaus came up to help Meges and got to Dolops’s side without being noticed. He speared him in the shoulder from behind, and the point, driven with great force, went through into his chest, and Dolops fell headlong. The two of them then went toward him to strip off his armor. But Hector called on all his brothers for help, and he especially reproached brave Melanippus son of Hiketaon. Before the war broke out, Melanippus used to pasture his herds of cattle in Percote. When the ships of the Danaans came, he went back to Ilium, where he was eminent among the Trojans and lived near Priam, who treated him like one of his own sons. Hector now rebuked him. “Why, Melanippus, are we so slack? Do you take no notice of the death of your kinsman? Do you not see how they are trying to take Dolops’s armor? Follow me. We must not fight the Argives from a distance now, but in close combat, until either we kill them or they take the high wall of Ilium and slay her people.”

He led the way as he spoke, and the hero Melanippus went after him. Meanwhile Ajax son of Telamon kept cheering on the Argives. “Be men, my friends,” he cried, “and dread disgrace. Behave in battle so that each of you earns the respect of the others. Men who care what their fellows think are less likely to be killed than men who do not. In flight there is neither gain nor glory.”

So he urged on men who were already set on driving back the Trojans. They took his words to heart and fenced the ships in as with a wall of bronze, while Zeus urged on the Trojans. Menelaus of the loud battle cry urged on Antilochus. “Antilochus,” he said, “you are young, and none of the Achaeans is more swift-footed or more valiant than you. See if you cannot spring upon some Trojan and kill him.”

Having spurred on Antilochus, Menelaus hurried away. Antilochus darted out at once from the front ranks, looked carefully around him, and threw a spear. The Trojans fell back as he threw, and the dart did not leave his hand in vain. It struck Melanippus, the proud son of Hiketaon, in the breast by the nipple as he was coming forward, and Melanippus fell heavily to the ground with his armor ringing and rattling around him. Antilochus sprang on him as a dog springs on a fawn that a hunter has hit as it broke from its hiding place, and killed it. In the same way, O Melanippus, stalwart Antilochus sprang on you to strip you of your armor. But noble Hector saw him and came running at him through the thick of the battle. Brave soldier though he was, Antilochus would not wait to face him. He fled like a savage creature that knows it has done wrong, and runs, after killing a dog or a man herding his cattle, before a crowd of men can gather to attack it. So the son of Nestor fled, and Hector and the Trojans showered their weapons after him with a cry that tore the air. He did not turn around and stop his flight until he had reached his comrades.

The Trojans, fierce as lions, kept rushing toward the ships to carry out the commands of Zeus. He kept spurring them on to new feats of daring, while he deadened the courage of the Argives and defeated them by encouraging the Trojans. For he meant to give glory to Hector son of Priam and let him throw fire upon the ships, until he had granted the unrighteous prayer that Thetis had made to him. So Zeus bided his time until he should see the glare of a blazing ship. From that hour he meant to arrange that the Trojans would be driven back from the ships and that the Achaeans would be given glory. With this purpose he inspired Hector son of Priam, who was eager enough already, to attack the ships. His fury was like that of Ares, or like a fire raging in the glades of a dense forest upon the mountains. He foamed at the mouth, his eyes glared under his terrible eyebrows, and his helmet quivered on his temples with the fury of his fighting. Zeus from heaven was with him, and though Hector was one man against many, Zeus granted him victory and glory. For he was doomed to an early death, and already Pallas Athena was hurrying on the hour of his destruction at the hands of the son of Peleus. For now, however, he kept trying to break the enemy ranks wherever he saw them thickest and in the finest armor. Whatever he did, he could not break through them, for they stood like a four-sided tower, or like a high cliff rising from the gray sea that stands against the anger of the gale and of the waves thundering up against it. He fell upon them like flames of fire from every side. A wave raised mountain high by wind and storm breaks over a ship and buries it deep in foam. The fierce winds roar against the mast, the sailors’ hearts fail them for fear, and they are saved from destruction by only a very little. In the same way the hearts of the Achaeans were fainting within them. Or think of a savage lion attacking a herd of cows feeding by the thousands in the low-lying meadows by some wide-watered shore. The herdsman is at his wit’s end how to protect his herd, and keeps going about, now in front of his cattle and now behind them, while the lion springs into the thick of them and fastens on a cow, so that they all tremble with fear. In the same way the Achaeans were utterly panic-stricken by Hector and father Zeus. Even so, Hector killed only Periphetes of Mycenae. He was the son of Copreus, who used to carry the orders of King Eurystheus to mighty Heracles, but the son was a far better man than his father in every way. He was swift-footed and a valiant warrior, and in understanding he ranked among the foremost men of Mycenae. It was he who gave Hector his triumph. As he turned back, he stumbled against the rim of his shield, which reached his feet and kept the javelins off him. He tripped on it and fell on his back, and his helmet rang loudly about his head as he fell. Hector saw him fall and ran up to him. He thrust a spear into his chest and killed him close to his own comrades. For all their sorrow, they could not help him, because they were themselves terribly afraid of Hector.

By now the Argives had reached the ships, and the prows of the ships drawn up first were on every side of them, but the Trojans came pouring after them. The Argives were driven back from the first row of ships, but they made a stand by their tents and did not break up and scatter. Shame and fear held them. They kept shouting to one another without stopping. Nestor of Gerene, tower of strength to the Achaeans, was loudest of all, begging every man by his parents to stand firm.

“Be men, my friends,” he cried, “and respect one another’s good opinion. Every one of you, think of your children, your wives, your property, and your parents, whether they are alive or dead. For their sake, though they are not here, I beg you to stand firm and not to turn in flight.”

With these words he put heart and soul into all of them. Athena took the thick veil of darkness away from their eyes, and a great light fell on them, on the side of the ships and on the side where the fight was raging alike. They could see Hector and all his men: those in the rear, who were taking no part in the battle, and those fighting by the ships.

Ajax could not bring himself to retreat with the rest. He strode from deck to deck with a great sea-pike in his hands, twelve cubits long and jointed with rings. A man skilled in feats of horsemanship couples four horses together and comes tearing at full speed along the public road from the country into some large town. Many men and women marvel as they watch him, because he keeps changing his horse, springing from one to another without ever missing his footing while the horses gallop. In the same way Ajax went striding from one ship’s deck to another, and his voice went up into the heavens. He kept shouting orders to the Danaans, urging them to defend their ships and tents. Hector, for his part, did not stay inside the main body of the Trojan warriors. A dun eagle swoops down on a flock of wild birds feeding near a river, geese, it may be, or cranes, or long-necked swans. In the same way Hector made straight for a dark-prowed ship and rushed right at it, for Zeus with his mighty hand drove him forward and roused his people to follow him.

Now the battle raged furiously at the ships again. You would have thought the men were coming on fresh and unwearied, so fiercely did they fight. This was the state of mind they were in. The Achaeans did not believe they would escape destruction but thought themselves doomed, while there was not a Trojan whose heart did not beat high with the hope of setting the ships on fire and putting the Achaean heroes to the sword.

That was how the two sides felt. Then Hector seized the stern of the good ship that had brought Protesilaus to Troy but never carried him back to his native land. Around this ship a close hand-to-hand fight raged between Danaans and Trojans. They did not fight at a distance with bows and javelins. With one mind they hacked at each other in close combat with their mighty swords and spears pointed at both ends. They also fought with keen battle-axes and with hatchets. Many a good stout blade, hilted and scabbarded with iron, fell from hand or shoulder as they fought, and the earth ran red with blood. Hector had seized the ship and would not let go. He held on to its curved stern and shouted to the Trojans, “Bring fire, and all of you raise the battle cry together. Zeus has granted us a day that will pay us back for all the rest. Today we shall take the ships that came here against the will of heaven, and that have caused us such endless suffering through the cowardice of our councillors. When I wanted to do battle at the ships, they held me back and forbade the army to follow me. If Zeus did then indeed warp our judgment, he himself now commands me and cheers me on.”

As he spoke, the Trojans sprang still more fiercely on the Achaeans. Ajax no longer held his ground. The darts flung at him overcame him, and he was sure he was doomed. So he left the raised deck at the stern and stepped back onto the seven-foot bench of the oarsmen. There he stood on the lookout, and with his spear he held back any Trojan he saw bringing fire to the ships. All the while he kept shouting at the top of his voice and urging on the Danaans. “My friends,” he cried, “Danaan heroes, servants of Ares, be men, my friends, and fight with all your might. Can we hope to find helpers later, or a wall to shield us more surely than the one we have? There is no strong city within reach from which we could draw fresh forces to turn the scales in our favor. We are on the plain of the armed Trojans with the sea behind us, far from our own country. Our salvation, therefore, is in the strength of our hands and in hard fighting.”

As he spoke, he wielded his spear with still greater fury. Whenever any Trojan made for the ships with fire at Hector’s bidding, Ajax was watching for him and drove at him with his long spear. In this way he killed twelve men in hand-to-hand fight before the ships.
